result.markdown: # Tutorial 2: Multiple regression and extensions {#i-ep02} ::: {.outcomes} By the end of Tutorial 2, you can - fit and interpret multiple regression in R; - test individual and grouped coefficients against zero; - interpret dummy, interaction, and polynomial terms correctly; - compare nested models with a partial F-test; - write a complete TestVision-ready analysis with design limits. ::: Tutorials are **exam preparation sessions**: every task below follows the format of the final exam. The standing routine for each task is the same --- the TA states the task, pairs work on it first for a few minutes with AI use allowed, and the solution is then discussed in plenary, starting from the pair attempts. One note on the order. The tasks run in course order: Task 1 rests on Lecture 4, Task 2 on Lecture 5, and Tasks 3--4 on yesterday's Lecture 6. This is deliberate --- the tutorial meets the day after Lecture 6, so you warm up on settled material before testing what you learned yesterday. ::: {.course-phase .phase-before} ## Before class Complete the after-class practice from Lectures 4--6. Use the complete [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet) while working, and review [Mathematics Refresher: multivariable equations, indicators, products, and powers](../resources/math-refresher.html) if needed. Complete from memory: 1. A multiple-regression slope is interpreted while ... 2. A dummy coefficient compares ... 3. An interaction coefficient is a difference in ... 4. A partial F-test compares ... ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your preparation 1. Holding the other included predictors fixed. 2. A category with the named reference category. 3. Slopes. 4. A reduced nested model with a complete model on the same observations. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-in-class} ## In class Attempt each task in R before opening the answer. All tasks use the Shark Tank teaching file and the running money unit of **thousands of dollars**. Build the analysis data once --- the same constructions as Lectures 4--6: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE) sharks$ask_1k <- sharks$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender <- subset(sharks, pitcher_gender_group != "unknown") known_gender$gender <- relevel(factor(known_gender$pitcher_gender_group), ref = "all_men") known_gender$ask_1k <- known_gender$ask_amount_usd / 1000 known_gender$women <- as.integer( known_gender$pitcher_gender_group %in% c("all_women", "mixed") ) known_gender$season_c <- known_gender$season - mean(known_gender$season) ``` ::: ### Task 1 --- Multiple-regression coefficients (Lecture 4) Fit: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m1 <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks ) summary(m1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + description_words, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.295 -4.776 -1.283 3.288 82.106 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 22.0249310 0.8878522 24.807 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8361515 0.0509825 -16.401 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0028975 0.0005771 -5.021 5.79e-07 *** description_words -0.1283379 0.1137527 -1.128 0.259 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.619 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1876, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1859 F-statistic: 110.6 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. Interpret all three slopes with units and conditioning. 2. Identify which 95% coefficient interval includes zero. 3. Interpret adjusted $R^2$ and the overall F-test. 4. State two threats to causal interpretation. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer At fixed values of the other included predictors, among the 1,441 recorded pitches: one later season is associated with about 0.836 percentage points less initial equity; an extra \$1,000 requested with about 0.0029 percentage points less equity (about 0.29 points per \$100,000); and one additional description word with about 0.128 percentage points less equity. The description-word interval, about $(-0.351,\; 0.095)$, includes zero. Adjusted $R^2\approx0.186$, and the overall F-test ($F\approx110.6$ on 3 and 1437 df) rejects the joint zero-slope null. Selection into the show, unmeasured venture quality, reverse relationships, and measurement choices are all possible causal threats. ::: ### Task 2 --- Dummy variables and a partial F-test (Lecture 5) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} reduced <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = known_gender) complete <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) summary(complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.118 -4.778 -1.100 3.220 82.590 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 20.8388333 0.5064929 41.143 < 2e-16 *** season -0.8238940 0.0477959 -17.238 < 2e-16 *** ask_1k -0.0026613 0.0005822 -4.571 5.28e-06 *** genderall_women 1.2835231 0.4810241 2.668 0.00771 ** gendermixed 0.1209343 0.5411539 0.223 0.82320 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.612 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1913, Adjusted R-squared: 0.189 F-statistic: 84.49 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(reduced, complete) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k + gender Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1431 83228 2 1429 82792 2 436.25 3.7649 0.0234 * --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. Name the reference category. 2. Interpret both dummy coefficients. 3. State and decide the partial F-test. 4. Explain why the partial test and the individual t-tests answer different questions. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer The reference is all-men. At the same season and requested amount, all-women presenting teams are fitted to offer about 1.28 equity percentage points more, and mixed teams about 0.12 points more, than all-men teams --- percentage points, not percent. The partial null is that both dummy coefficients equal zero; $F\approx3.76$, p $\approx$ 0.023, so reject at 5%: the terms are jointly useful even though the mixed dummy's own t-test (p $\approx$ 0.82) is far from significant. The F-test asks whether the pair improves the model together; each t-test asks about one reference-group contrast. The broad source coding and observational design prohibit a causal gender claim. ::: ### Task 3 --- Interaction (Lecture 6) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_interaction <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) summary(m_interaction) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season_c * women + ask_1k, data = known_gender) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -15.871 -4.742 -1.290 3.412 82.689 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 13.6247907 0.3354522 40.616 < 2e-16 *** season_c -0.7993817 0.0663226 -12.053 < 2e-16 *** women 0.8069665 0.4117061 1.960 0.0502 . ask_1k -0.0026776 0.0005834 -4.590 4.83e-06 *** season_c:women -0.0614594 0.0955667 -0.643 0.5203 --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.62 on 1429 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1894, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1871 F-statistic: 83.47 on 4 and 1429 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ::: 1. Write the fitted line for `women = 0` and `women = 1` at a fixed request. 2. Calculate both season slopes. 3. Interpret the interaction estimate and p-value without overclaiming in either direction. 4. Explain the role of centering. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer For all-men teams the season slope is about $-0.799$ percentage points per season; for teams with women represented it is $-0.799-0.061=-0.861$. The estimated slope difference is $-0.061$ percentage points per season with p $\approx$ 0.520: this model provides no evidence of different season trends between the two source-defined groups --- and no proof of equal trends, since the estimate is imprecise. Centering makes the lower-order group coefficient compare the groups at the average season (about 8.8) instead of at the unobserved Season 0; it changes neither the fitted values nor the interaction estimate. ::: ### Task 4 --- Polynomial term (Lecture 6) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} m_linear <- lm(equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k, data = sharks) m_quadratic <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks ) summary(m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Call: lm(formula = equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k, data = sharks) Residuals: Min 1Q Median 3Q Max -16.154 -4.549 -1.011 3.390 82.000 Coefficients: Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|) (Intercept) 24.171681 0.820566 29.457 < 2e-16 *** season -1.713233 0.205669 -8.330 < 2e-16 *** I(season^2) 0.051034 0.011369 4.489 7.74e-06 *** ask_1k -0.002711 0.000574 -4.723 2.56e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 Residual standard error: 7.57 on 1437 degrees of freedom Multiple R-squared: 0.1981, Adjusted R-squared: 0.1965 F-statistic: 118.3 on 3 and 1437 DF, p-value: < 2.2e-16 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} anova(m_linear, m_quadratic) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Analysis of Variance Table Model 1: equity_offered_pct ~ season + ask_1k Model 2: equity_offered_pct ~ season + I(season^2) + ask_1k Res.Df RSS Df Sum of Sq F Pr(>F) 1 1438 83493 2 1437 82338 1 1154.5 20.149 7.737e-06 *** --- Signif. codes: 0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1 ``` ::: ::: 1. Why must `I(season^2)` be used in the R formula? 2. Decide whether the quadratic term adds fit under the classical test. 3. Calculate the fitted change from Season 10 to Season 11. 4. State why the curve should not be extrapolated beyond Season 16. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check your answer `I()` tells R to square arithmetically rather than read `^` as formula syntax. The partial F-test gives $F\approx20.1$ with p $<$ 0.001, so the quadratic term adds detectable fit. With $b_1\approx-1.713$ and $b_2\approx0.051$, the change from Season 10 to 11 is $b_1+b_2(2\times10+1)=b_1+21b_2\approx-0.64$ percentage points --- never read $b_1$ alone while the squared term is in the model. Beyond Season 16 the fitted parabola turns upward with no data support; polynomials can behave sharply outside the observed range. ::: ::: ::: {.course-phase .phase-after} ## After class ### Timed integrated task --- 30 minutes Develop one model of `equity_offered_pct` using season, the requested amount in $1,000s, the three known source gender groups, and one justified extension. Your submission must include: 1. a precise research question; 2. reproducible data preparation; 3. one pre-model visual; 4. the R formula and model summary; 5. coefficient interpretations with units and reference groups; 6. an individual t-test and an overall or partial F-test; 7. $R^2$, adjusted $R^2$, and residual diagnostics; 8. one graph of fitted conditional predictions; 9. a 150-word conclusion separating association, uncertainty, and causal limits. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## Check a model structure A defensible solution could fit ```r m <- lm( equity_offered_pct ~ season * gender + ask_1k, data = known_gender ) ``` or a quadratic-season model with group dummies. Keep lower-order terms, name the reference group, interpret combined slopes or fitted contrasts, compare a nested reduced model with `anova(reduced, complete)`, inspect residuals (including `rstandard()` and Cook's distance), and plot predictions within Seasons 1--16. The conclusion must state that the source's broad presenter classification and the selected televised records do not identify a causal effect of gender or season. ::: ### Make it yours (5 minutes) :::: {.utility-prompt} Utility: two sentences Think of your EiA3 venture --- or any business you know well. Sketch, in two sentences, the integrated analysis you would actually run on its data: first name the outcome, two predictors, and the one extension (a dummy set, an interaction, or a quadratic) that a real question motivates, then say which single caveat --- selection, measurement, or omitted variables --- would headline your 150-word conclusion. There is no wrong answer; the point is noticing that you now own the entire pipeline. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true"} ## See an example, then write your own Take a student-run campus meal-prep box venture. "Outcome: weekly orders; predictors: ad spend and price, plus an exam-week dummy interacted with ad spend, because I believe ads work mainly when students are on campus. The headlining caveat is omitted variables: weather drives both my flyer effort and campus foot traffic, and nothing in my data measures it." ::: You can discuss this task --- and any other task in this tutorial --- with **Tilly**, the course AI assistant on Canvas: ask it to referee your two-sentence design before you invest a weekend in the data. :::: QM Intermediate is complete. Review the [QM Intermediate Code Sheet](#intermediate-code-sheet), attempt the [QM Intermediate Mock Exam](#intermediate-mock-exam), then return to the [R Refresher](../resources/r-refresher.html), [Mathematics Refresher](../resources/math-refresher.html), or the [External Video Guide](../resources/video-guide.html) whenever you need a targeted review. :::
